item.title: Attempt to erase Tagore portrait: Four remanded, including ANM Ayas
item.description:
A Dhaka court on Sunday remanded 4 people, including State Dialogue Forum Member Secretary ANM Ayas, in a case filed over an attempt to erase a portrait of Rabindranath Tagore painted on a wall in front of the Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy in Segunbagicha.
The court granted 3 days of remand for Ayas and Sakibul Hasan and 2 days each for Sujon Mia and Marjia Khandaker Rimi.
Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Jashita Islam passed the order following an application by the investigation officer. Assistant Sub-Inspector (ASI) Md Rezaul Karim of the police prosecution department confirmed the remand orders.
Earlier, Shahbagh police station Sub-Inspector (SI) Abdul Gaffar Himel, the investigation officer, produced the 4 accused before the court and sought 10 days of remand.
Dhaka Metropolitan Public Prosecutor Omar Faruk Faruqi argued in favor of remand on behalf of the state. Defense lawyer Monir Hossain sought cancellation of the remand petitions and bail for the accused.
On Saturday, SI Ziaul Haque of Shahbagh police station filed the case over the attempted erasure of Tagore's portrait. The accused have been charged with criminal conspiracy, creating enmity between different groups and hurting religious sentiments.
At noon on Saturday, a group of young people, including Ayas, faced police obstruction while attempting to erase Tagore's portrait on a wall in front of the Shilpakala Academy. An argument broke out between the 2 sides, after which police detained Ayas and 3 others and took them to the police station.
At the scene, a woman was seen applying ink to Tagore's portrait before a police officer intervened to stop her. The woman said they had come to protest against “Indian aggression.”
The group also chanted slogans under Ayas's leadership after facing police obstruction.
On October 5, Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) cleared the footpath in Segunbagicha of encroachments. Portraits of 10 prominent figures who contributed to art, literature and culture were subsequently painted on the wall beside the footpath.
Those depicted included Rabindranath Tagore, National Poet Kazi Nazrul Islam, Shilpacharya Zainul Abedin, Satyajit Ray and Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar.
On Friday, a Facebook page named “July Revolutionary Alliance” questioned the decision to paint the portraits. The post criticized the inclusion of Satyajit Ray and Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar, describing them as “cultural figures of West Bengal.”
The following day, a group of people led by Ayas attempted to erase the portraits.

item.title: Saudi-bound Bangladeshis stranded as airport attacks disrupt flights
item.description:
Saudi-bound Bangladeshi expatriates have been left stranded and uncertain after attacks on Saudi airports forced the cancellation of flights between Dhaka and Riyadh.
Five flights from Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport have so far been cancelled, affecting 2,532 passengers, according to the Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB).
The cancelled flights include services operated by Biman Bangladesh Airlines, US-Bangla Airlines, Saudia, Riyadh Air and SriLankan Airlines.
The disruptions have left passengers unable to travel to Saudi Arabia, while expatriates there are also struggling to return home. Many passengers travelled long distances from different parts of the country to reach Dhaka airport, only to learn that their flights had been cancelled. Most had booked their tickets through travel agencies in Saudi Arabia and were unsure when or how their travel dates would be rescheduled.
Many are also worried about losing their jobs if they fail to return to their workplaces on time. The cancellations have also increased their transportation, accommodation and food expenses.
Passengers waiting for Riyadh-bound flights were seen at airline counters with their tickets and travel documents, seeking information about their next steps. Others were calling family members amid growing uncertainty over their travel plans.
Akbar Hossain, a Riyadh-bound passenger, said he was scheduled to fly on Saturday but could not travel due to the situation.
“I don't know what to do now. If I cannot return on time, I will face problems. We will be in serious trouble if the situation is not resolved soon,” he said outside the airport's departure terminal.
Sharif Uddin of Brahmanbaria was also scheduled to travel to Riyadh on an IndiGo flight via Mumbai. However, the current situation has left his travel plans uncertain.
Meanwhile, expatriates in Saudi Arabia have also been unable to return to Bangladesh amid the flight disruptions. Airline officials said some passengers were still at the affected airports and had been asked to leave amid the prevailing situation.
Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport Executive Director SM Ragib Samad said the seven cancelled flights were scheduled to carry 2,532 passengers to Riyadh.
“The concerned airlines are informing the affected passengers. Passengers are requested to contact their respective airlines to confirm their rescheduled travel plans,” he said.
“This is a global crisis. We urge everyone to remain patient and show empathy until the situation returns to normal,” he added.
Earlier, a missile attack by the Houthis on Riyadh's international airport late Saturday night reportedly killed at least 12 people and injured 309 others. The casualties included citizens of Bangladesh, Egypt, Jordan, Palestine, Sudan, Syria and the United States.
Following the attack, all operations at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport were suspended.

item.title: Police chief orders action against misleading posts ahead of Durga Puja
item.description:
Inspector General of Police (IGP) Md Ali Hossain Fakir on Sunday ordered police officials to take immediate action against misleading social media posts, rumors and propaganda aimed at disrupting communal harmony during Durga Puja, saying adequate security measures have been taken to ensure peaceful celebrations across the country.
Police have adopted a three-tier security arrangement covering the pre-Puja period, the festival and idol immersion and post-Puja activities, he said while speaking at a meeting on law and order and security arrangements for Durga Puja at the Police Headquarters.
The IGP urged everyone to remain alert and vigilant to prevent any individual or group from disrupting communal harmony during the festival.
He also stressed strengthening public engagement through community policing and beat policing.
Expressing hope that Durga Puja would be celebrated safely and joyfully as in previous years, the IGP called for collective efforts to maintain a peaceful atmosphere.
The meeting was attended by heads of different police units based in Dhaka and other relevant officials.
Metropolitan police commissioners, range deputy inspectors general, district police superintendents and the superintendent of police of river police joined the meeting virtually.
Police officials were also directed to maintain regular contact with prominent members of different religious communities and local residents, as well as conduct regular visits to Puja mandaps to ensure security.
The police administration said it was working to prevent any untoward incidents during the celebrations.
Leaders of Puja celebration committees were urged to contact the national emergency service 999 or the nearest police station if they encountered any situation requiring immediate attention.
The IGP also called on the organizers to keep CCTV cameras operational, ensure adequate lighting at Puja mandaps and idol immersion sites, arrange standby generators and deploy volunteers at every mandap to maintain round-the-clock security.
Uniformed and plainclothes police personnel, along with Special Weapons and Tactics (SWAT), Crime Response Teams (CRT), Quick Response Teams (QRT), crime scene vans and bomb disposal units, will remain on standby to respond to any emergency during the festival.
Round-the-clock monitoring cells will also operate at Police Headquarters and other police units throughout the celebrations.
This year, around 33,000 Puja mandaps are hosting Durga Puja celebrations across the country.

item.title: Sajek road blockade disrupts tourist travel, 2,500 visitors stranded
item.description:
An indefinite road blockade in Sajek, Baghaichhari, Rangamati, disrupted transport between Sajek and Dighinala on Sunday, leaving around 2,500 tourists facing uncertainty over their return journey.
The blockade was called by the Sajek Public Rights Protection Committee and the Sajek Karbari Association, with protesters demanding the arrest of individuals accused of creating instability in the area.
According to local sources, protesters have been staging demonstrations by burning tires at several points along the Sajek-Dighinala road, including Gangaram and Ujor Bazar, since Sunday morning. Vehicle movement from Sajek and Baghaichhari toward Dighinala has been halted.
The blockade was announced in a press release issued on Saturday afternoon and signed by Bijoy Kanti Chakma, member secretary of the Sajek Public Rights Protection Committee.
The press release alleged that an armed group using the name of the Parbatya Chattagram Jana Samhati Samiti (PCJSS) had been creating an unstable situation in Sajek and subjecting ordinary people to threats and intimidation. It said the blockade was intended to demand the arrest of those involved and measures to protect the lives and property of local residents.
Bijoy Kanti Chakma said: “Fed up with the oppression by terrorists using the PCJSS name, we have decided to impose this blockade. Our movement will continue until the government takes visible legal action against them.”
Meanwhile, Md Yasin Arafat, a line manager at the Sajek tourist center, said 90 vehicles, including cars, larger vehicles and motorcycles, entered Sajek on Saturday with the government security convoy, or escort. More than 900 tourists arrived in the area in those vehicles.
Rahul Chakma John, organizing secretary of the Cottage and Resort Owners Association (CROA) of Sajek, said around 2,500 tourists were staying in Sajek.
Although the blockade had disrupted regular travel, he said there was a possibility of arranging an escorted departure for tourists from Sajek at around 2pm on Sunday.
He also expressed hope that arrangements could be made for new tourists to enter Sajek at the same time.
Md Toffazzal Hossain, officer-in-charge of Sajek police station, said the blockade had proceeded peacefully since morning, with no reports of untoward.

item.title: PM monitoring situation of Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is closely monitoring the situation of Bangladeshis affected by a missile attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, which has reportedly killed 12 people, including two Bangladeshis.
Sources at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the Bangladesh Embassy in Riyadh was in contact with Saudi authorities to gather information about the victims and assess the situation.
A foreign ministry official said Bangladeshis who escaped unharmed had been relocated to two hotels. The prime minister is keeping a close watch on developments, the official added.
According to sources, a group of 41 Bangladeshi Umrah pilgrims were waiting at the airport to travel from Riyadh to Jeddah when an explosion rocked the terminal.
Two of those killed have been identified as Bangladeshis, but their identities were not immediately available. Eleven people remain missing, and officials suspect the death toll could rise.
The pilgrims are reportedly teachers at Jamia Arabia Rabiul Ulum, a madrasa in Kamrangirchar, Dhaka.
Several others were injured and are receiving treatment at local hospitals. The exact number of casualties remains unconfirmed.

item.title: PM invites Marubeni to invest in IT, fertilizer, energy sectors
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Sunday invited Japanese business conglomerate Marubeni Corporation to invest in Bangladesh's information technology (IT), fertiliser and energy sectors, highlighting his government's moves to harness the country's economic potential and attract domestic and foreign investment.
The premier made the invitation when a high-level delegation led by Marubeni Corporation President and CEO Masayuki Omoto paid a courtesy call on him at his office at the Bangladesh Secretariat in the morning, said his Deputy Press Secretary Shahadat Shadhin.
During the meeting, the prime minister highlighted the longstanding business ties between Bangladesh and Marubeni in jute products and stressed the need to expand the existing relationship and strengthen cooperation in new sectors, Shadhin said.
The discussions covered investment opportunities in information technology (IT), artificial intelligence (AI), cybersecurity, fertiliser and energy, as well as the possibility of establishing a second Karnaphuli Fertilizer Company Limited (KAFCO) plant in Bangladesh.
The two sides also discussed the potential of Bangladesh's IT sector, the development of skilled human resources and the country's prospects for becoming an international service hub.
Tarique Rahman highlighted the government's plan to enhance the skills of Bangladeshi engineering graduates in IT and cybersecurity. Bangladesh could emerge as a major international service hub by leveraging its skilled workforce,
technological capabilities and competitive service offerings, the meeting observed.
The possibility of launching an AI-powered data centre in Bangladesh within the next 12 months also came up for discussion, along with potential investment and technological cooperation from Marubeni in the project.
The meeting also discussed expanding the use of modern technologies and AI in agriculture to improve agricultural production and management, including through Marubeni's potential investment and technical assistance.
On fertiliser production, the two sides discussed expanding Marubeni's existing investment in KAFCO and the possibility of setting up a second KAFCO plant in the country. Marubeni expressed interest in the proposal, Shadhin said.
The meeting also expressed optimism that the Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA) between Bangladesh and Japan, once implemented, would further strengthen trade and investment ties between the two countries.
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam, Prime Minister's Adviser on Information and Technology Rehan Asif Asad and Special Assistant to the Prime Minister Dr Md Shakirul Islam Khan were present.
Marubeni was represented by its Chief Executive Officer for Southwest Asia Susumu Wakamori and the company's Country Head in Bangladesh Manabu Sugawara.

item.title: Bank Asia organizes cybersecurity awareness training for employees
item.description:
Bank Asia PLC organized a daylong training program to raise cybersecurity awareness among its employees and enhance their skills in protecting the bank’s digital assets.
The training was arranged in observance of National Cybersecurity Awareness Month.
Md Sabbir Hossain, additional managing director of Bank Asia PLC, inaugurated the program at the Bank Asia Institute for Training and Development (BAITD) in Lalmatia, Dhaka on October 10.
SM Tofayel Ahmad, additional director (ICT) of Bangladesh Bank, conducted the training session.
The session covered key aspects of cybersecurity governance, regulatory expectations, management responsibilities, cybersecurity risks, threat, employee responsibilities and good security practices.
Team leaders of different levels, including the heads of various departments and branches of the bank, attended the program in person, while other employees participated online.

item.title: CID, bKash held series workshops on cyber awareness for 1,100 female students
item.description:
The Criminal Investigation Department (CID) and bKash have jointly organized a series of awareness workshops on cyber security and secure financial transactions for female students of Viqarunnisa Noon School and College and Dhaka University's Ruqayyah and Shamsun Nahar halls.
Around 1,100 students joined these sessions, where officials from Cyber Police Centre (CPC) of CID and External Affairs Department of bKash shared practical insights on safeguarding personal information in digital space and avoiding fraudulent traps in digital financial services.
The sessions highlighted guidelines for the safe use of Mobile Financial Services (MFS) alongside real-life case studies of cyber risks.
Key discussions focused on maintaining strict confidentiality over PINs or OTPs, identifying phishing links disguised as lucrative offers, and reporting suspicious activities promptly through official channels.
Experts also urged participants to fact-check online content before sharing to prevent the spread of rumours and misinformation.
The first session was held at Viqarunnisa Noon School and College, engaging around 650 students.
Md Jahidul Islam, Additional DIG of the Cyber Police Centre, CID, discussed various forms of cybercrime, personal data security, and risk mitigation strategies.
Sana Shaminur Rahman, DIG of CPC, CID, graced the occasion as chief guest, while Major AKM Monirul Karim (retd.), EVP and head of external affairs at bKash, was present as the special guest.
The outreach then moved to the University of Dhaka, engaging 450 students across two sessions at Ruqayyah Hall and Shamsun Nahar Hall.
Md Shafiuddin Shaheen, DIG (Acting), CPC, CID, joined both sessions as chief guest.
The events were presided over by Ruqayyah Hall Provost Prof Dr Hosne Ara Begum and Shamsun Nahar Hall Provost Prof Dr Nasrin Sultana, respectively.
Organizers stated that similar awareness workshops will be expanded to other educational institutions across the country in phases.
While advanced technology and active law enforcement are vital, a secure digital financial ecosystem ultimately relies on vigilant, well-informed users.
With this goal in mind, bKash has been organizing regular awareness workshops since 2017 with the law enforcement authorities (Police, DB, CID, PBI) for investigating officials and bKash agents.
Aiming to secure a safer digital future, a dedicated drive has now been launched to educate young students, which will be rolled out across educational institutions nationwide.

item.title: Midland Bank launches Bangla QR service to promote cashless transactions
item.description:
Midland Bank PLC (MDB) recently launched Bangla QR services at selected retail merchant locations across the country.
This initiative is part of the bank's ongoing commitment to promoting digital payments and fostering a cashless Bangladesh.
Imtiaz U Ahmed, managing director of Midland Bank PLC, officially inaugurated the Bangla QR service, joined by senior officials of the bank.
Bangla QR enables customers to make convenient payments by scanning a merchant's QR code using compatible mobile banking applications and digital payment platforms.
This service is designed to simplify everyday transactions, making them faster and more convenient, while simultaneously reducing reliance on cash.
Speaking at the launch, Imtiaz U Ahmed stated: "The introduction of Bangla QR marks another significant step in Midland Bank's digital transformation journey. Through this service, we aim to encourage both customers and merchants to embrace secure and convenient digital payments, thereby contributing to Bangladesh's transition towards a cashless economy."
Through this initiative, Midland Bank seeks to integrate more retail merchants into the digital payment ecosystem and encourage broader adoption of QR-based transactions nationwide.
The bank is committed to expanding its Bangla QR merchant network and enhancing its digital payment services, aligning with Bangladesh Bank's efforts to cultivate an inclusive and cashless payment ecosystem.
Also present at the inauguration were Md Zahid Hossain, deputy managing director & CRO; Md Nazmul Huda Sarkar, deputy managing director & CTO; and other senior officials of Midland Bank.

item.title: NCC Bank holds nationwide training program for women entrepreneurs
item.description:
NCC Bank is organizing a nationwide training program on “Entrepreneurship Development & Green Banking” with the aim of promoting women’s economic empowerment, financial inclusion, entrepreneurship development, and sustainable business practices.
The program is being implemented as part of the bank’s continued initiatives to enhance the business knowledge and skills of women entrepreneurs while making banking and financing facilities more accessible to them.
The training program is being conducted through NCC Bank’s extensive network of branches and sub-branches across the country.
With a target of training 3,000 women entrepreneurs, the program has already been completed at 99 branches, with a total of 2,490 women entrepreneurs participating in the training sessions.
As part of the initiative, a training session was recently organized at NCC Bank Dhanmondi Branch, where Md Habibur Rahman, deputy managing director of NCC Bank, attended as chief guest.
Nighat Mumtaz, EVP & head of sustainable & women’s banking, and Md Jashimuddin, SVP & regional head of Outskirts Dhaka Region, were present as special guests.
Helal Uddin, VP & HoBB of Elephant Road Branch, chaired the program.
Md Habibur Rahman, deputy managing director of NCC Bank, encouraged women customers to open Parama Accounts and take advantage of NCC Bank’s dedicated women’s banking facilities and services.
He said that women entrepreneurs play a vital role in strengthening the national economy, generating employment, and promoting inclusive economic growth.
He emphasized that access to formal financial services, appropriate financing, digital banking facilities, and practical business knowledge is essential for enabling women entrepreneurs to establish, manage, and expand sustainable businesses.
He highlighted NCC Bank’s digital banking initiatives, including NCC Always, Digital Account Opening, and Bangla QR, which make banking and business transactions more accessible, convenient, and efficient.
He encouraged women entrepreneurs to make greater use of these digital facilities to manage their financial activities, streamline business transactions, and benefit from modern banking services.
Nighat Mumtaz, EVP & head of sustainable & women’s banking of NCC Bank, said the bank is committed to empowering women entrepreneurs through financing, knowledge-sharing, training, and capacity-building initiatives.
She said the nationwide training program, being conducted across the Bank’s branch network, aims to enhance women entrepreneurs’ practical knowledge of entrepreneurship development and green banking while promoting sustainable business practices.
She highlighted NCC Bank’s Green Banking Refinance facilities and Parama’s Conventional and Islamic Banking products, offering women entrepreneurs tailored financial solutions at attractive rates.
She emphasized that access to finance, knowledge, and modern banking services can help women entrepreneurs strengthen and expand their businesses and contribute more actively to the formal economy.

item.title: NRB Bank holds Annual Risk Conference 2026
item.description:
NRB Bank PLC convened its Annual Risk Conference 2026 on 10 October 2026 in a hybrid arrangement at a Club Notredamians Bangladesh Limited, Banani-10, Dhaka as part of the bank’s commitment towards building awareness of risk, to establish robust risk management culture and to be compliant with regulatory directives.
The theme of this year’s risk conference was “Risk Management as part of Bankers’ DNA”.
The conference was graced by Istequemal Hussain, director (BSD-10), Bangladesh Bank, as chief guest; Mohammad Abdur Rab, director (SPCD), Bangladesh Bank, as special guest & resource person; and Md Mahfuzur Rahman, additional director (BSD-10), Bangladesh Bank as resource person.
The conference was hosted by Tarek Reaz Khan, managing director & CEO, NRB Bank PLC.
All other members of senior management and divisional heads of the bank physically participated in the conference; while representatives of all branches and sub-branches all over the country of the bank joined the conference on digital platform.
Istequemal Hussain, director (BSD-10), Bangladesh Bank highlighted the importance of risk management in long term sustainable banking operation and thanked the Management of NRB Bank for addressing the spirit of the age “Risk Management as part of Bankers’ DNA” as core theme of the conference.
Mohammad Abdur Rab, director (SPCD), Bangladesh Bank highlighted insightful discussions on risk-based supervision, regulatory compliance, risk identification and mitigation strategies, emphasizing the importance of embedding risk awareness and accountability into everyday banking practices.
Md Mahfuzur Rahman, additional director (BSD-10), Bangladesh Bank discusses on the major areas where NRB Bank need to focus for resiliency.
Tarek Reaz Khan, managing director & CEO, NRB Bank PLC discusses on the importance of risk culture, regulatory compliance and practice of good governance in the bank.
He discussed about the importance and impacts of the “Tone of the Top” culture in the bank’s risk governance and the significance of risk escalation towards developing NRB Bank as a risk focused sustainable bank.
He also urged all concerned officials to be more cautious in the challenging environment and be a prudent risk manager of his/her respective desk.
Through this initiative, NRB Bank PLC. reaffirmed its commitment to strengthening corporate governance, promoting a proactive risk management culture and ensuring sustainable banking practices in line with Bangladesh Bank's regulatory guidelines.

item.title: Durga idol made with 1.5 lakh matchsticks draws crowds in Satkhira
item.description:
A Durga idol crafted from more than 150,000 matchsticks and over 10kg of silk thread has become a major attraction ahead of this year’s Sharadiya Durga Puja in Satkhira.
The unusual idol, created at the Dhulihar-Brahmarajpur Sri Sri Durga Puja Mandap in Satkhira Sadar, is drawing visitors eager to admire its intricate craftsmanship.
With Mahalaya observed on Friday, marking the beginning of the festive season, temples and puja mandaps across the district are bustling with activity as artisans put the finishing touches to idols and decorations.
At the Brahmarajpur temple, more than 150,000 matchsticks have been meticulously attached to a clay idol to create elaborate patterns requiring exceptional precision and patience. Even a minor mistake could ruin the design, making the work particularly challenging.
Idol maker Nabodip Sarkar said he had seen similar artwork in Kolkata in 2023 and decided to introduce the technique in Satkhira.
Four artisans have been working around the clock, sometimes until 2am or 3am, to complete the idol, he said. Sarkar has also been commissioned to make Durga idols at four locations this year, including in Satkhira and Kushtia.
He said special adhesives and chemicals had been used to neutralise the combustible properties of the match heads, with precautions taken to minimise safety risks.
Amit Kumar Ghosh, assistant treasurer of the Brahmarajpur Sarbojanin Sri Sri Durga Mandir committee, said the artisans’ fees alone amounted to around Tk1.3 lakh, while the total budget for this year’s celebrations was approximately Tk5 lakh.
The puja, organised by zamindar Pashupati Mitra, has been celebrated for more than 200 years, he said.
Unconventional idols have become something of a tradition at the temple. Last year, an idol made with 100kg of Chinigura rice attracted visitors from far and wide. Encouraged by the response, the organisers decided to experiment with another unusual material this year.
Safety concerns surrounding the matchstick idol prompted an inspection and trial on September 16 involving Satkhira Sadar Upazila Nirbahi Officer Arnab Kumar Dutta, the officer-in-charge of Satkhira Sadar police station and officials from Fire Service and Civil Defence.
Closed-circuit television cameras have also been installed throughout the temple premises to ensure the safety of the idol and visitors.
Preparations are underway at puja mandaps across the district, including in Shyamnagar, Kaliganj, Debhata, Assasuni, Tala and Kalaroa. Alongside traditional clay idols built over bamboo and straw frameworks, artisans are experimenting with different decorative designs.
The festival also provides employment for potters, bamboo and wood craftsmen, painters and decoration workers.
Biswanath Ghosh, general secretary of the Satkhira district unit of the Bangladesh Puja Udjapan Parishad, said 590 puja mandaps would host celebrations in the district this year, up from 587 last year.
Mahalaya on Friday marked the beginning of the countdown to the festival. Maha Shashthi will be observed on October 17, while the celebrations will conclude with Bijoya Dashami on October 21.
According to Hindu tradition, the goddess will arrive on horseback and depart by boat this year.

item.title: Gopalganj university school faces existential crisis
item.description:
Gopalganj Science and Technology University School and College is facing an uncertain future as its teachers and employees have gone without salaries and allowances for about seven years, while students struggle with inadequate classrooms, poor sanitation, unsafe drinking water, and the lack of a playground.
Established on the university campus in 2017, the school initially had 16 teachers and three employees and enrolled 675 students in its first year. The college section was never opened.
The teachers and employees have not been receiving salaries and allowances since 2019. The school received academic recognition from the Dhaka Education Board in 2020.
It was later relocated from beside the university library to an area near the vice-chancellor’s residence. Teachers, students, and guardians said its condition deteriorated after the relocation, causing enrolment to decline. The school now has only 160 students from pre-primary to Class 10.
Students said classrooms lack adequate fans and roofs leak during rain. They also complained about poor sanitation and a lack of safe drinking water.
“There are bushes near the washrooms where snakes are seen. Water also leaks through the classroom roof when it rains,” said Class 5 student Fariduzzaman Ahsaf.
Class 7 student Riyan said the school had no playground and students had to attend classes in extreme heat.
Guardians said teachers’ dedication was the main reason they continued sending their children to the school. Saila Zaman, mother of a Class 6 student, said the campus environment was good but facilities were inadequate. “Two classes are sometimes held in the same room. There are not enough fans, and there are many other problems,” she said.
Assistant teacher Aleya Begum said teachers had been running the school with money collected from students and contributions from their own pockets. “We have not received salaries or allowances for nearly seven years. It has become extremely difficult to support our families. Some teachers travel from Khulna, Kotalipara and other areas to attend school regularly,” she said.
Vice-Chancellor Prof Dr Md Sohel Hasan said the school had no formal approval and was not included in the university’s organogram. “There is a school here with teachers, employees and students. I will form a committee to include it in the organogram and then seek University Grants Commission approval for appointing teachers and employees,” he said.
The vice-chancellor further said he would take necessary steps to resolve the school’s problems and improve educational opportunities for the students.

item.title: Malaysian national jailed after remand in 4.5kg gold case
item.description:
A Malaysian national arrested with 4.5kg of gold worth nearly Tk8 crore at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka has been sent to jail after a six-day remand.
On Sunday, investigation officer SI Mahbub Hossain of Airport Police Station produced Yang Don Seow, 43, before the court and sought an order to send him to jail. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Kamal Uddin passed the order to send him jail following the petition.
SI Abu Bakar Siddique of the prosecution division confirmed the matter, adding that the accused had not sought bail.
The court had placed him on a six-day remand last Monday.
He was arrested around 4:00am on October 4 after customs officials recovered nine gold bars weighing a total of 4.5kg from him. The gold was valued at approximately Tk7.95 crore, according to the National Board of Revenue (NBR).
The NBR said Yang arrived in Dhaka from Kuala Lumpur on Malaysia Airlines flight MH0196. Customs officials monitored him after the flight landed and searched him as he passed through Green Channel-1 after collecting his baggage.
The recovered gold comprised four bars weighing 1kg each and five weighing 100g each. The 24-carat gold bars were concealed under his shirt in a black cloth belt.
Assistant Revenue Officer Moniruzzaman of the Dhaka Customs House's Customs Preventive unit filed a case against him under the Special Powers Act at Airport Police Station on Sunday.

item.title: Sobhana’s historic ton lifts Bangladesh to 220 against Australia in second ODI
item.description:
Sobhana Mostary struck a historic century as Bangladesh Women recovered from a disastrous start to post 220 for six in their second ODI against Australia Women in Brisbane on Sunday.
The right-handed batter scored 118 off 134 balls, hitting 18 boundaries, to register Bangladesh’s highest individual score in any format of women’s international cricket. Her magnificent innings also helped the visitors record their highest total against Australia in women’s ODIs.
Sent in to bat after Australia captain Tahlia McGrath won the toss and elected to field, Bangladesh suffered a nightmare start, losing three wickets for just eight runs inside the first eight overs.
Fargana Hoque fell for a 13-ball duck, while Sarmin Sultana managed five and Sharmin Akhter was dismissed without scoring as Australia’s bowlers capitalised on the early movement and bounce.
With Bangladesh in deep trouble, Sobhana joined captain Nigar Sultana Joty at the crease to stage a remarkable recovery. The pair negotiated the early challenges and gradually built a commanding partnership, putting pressure back on the hosts with a combination of solid defence and positive strokeplay.
Sobhana brought up her half-century off 66 balls before reaching her maiden ODI hundred off 123 deliveries. Her knock was the cornerstone of a 195-run fourth-wicket partnership with Joty, the highest women’s ODI stand at the Brisbane ground.
Reflecting on her innings, Sobhana credited the support of her coaches and teammates for helping her maintain her composure under pressure.
“Actually, I'm so happy because of my hundred, and I would like to thank my coaches, my teammates, and my friends also. They supported me so much. They were always telling me, ‘Hey, you stay, you play your game.’ So I just stuck to my plan and played my positive shots,” she said.
Sobhana added that Joty had encouraged her to build a long partnership after the early collapse.
“She told me, ‘You just stay here, you and me just stay and play a long innings.’ My coach also told me to bat longer, so that was the plan,” she said.
The partnership ended in the 48th over when Sobhana was bowled by Megan Schutt for 118, with Bangladesh at 203. Joty remained unbeaten on 74 off 114 balls, including seven fours, as Schutt finished with four wickets for 36 runs.
Bangladesh lost three wickets in the closing stages but reached 220 for six, scoring 212 runs after losing their third wicket.
Head coach David Hemp said the team needed greater exposure to challenging conditions, particularly the extra bounce in Australia, but stressed that the players had demonstrated their potential.
“We want to be exposed to this all the time, and if we are, as you can see, they can do it. But it's about consistency, and that exposure is really important,” Hemp said.
Australia need 221 runs to win the second ODI.

item.title: New Zealand confirm split ODI squads for India series
item.description:
Rachin Ravindra and Mark Chapman were named on Sunday in New Zealand's squad for their home one-day series against India after injury sidelined the batting pair from the preceding Twenty20 clashes.
Coach Rob Walter named an enlarged group of 21 players for five ODI matches in November, which follows five T20s.
Only six will play the entire series, including captain Mitchell Santner, while eight others will be involved in the first three games before leaving to prepare for two Tests against the tourists.
Seven players will then come in for the two final ODIs.
Left-hander Ravindra was ruled out of the T20s after dislocating his shoulder when diving to take a catch during a promotional event last month.
Likewise, Chapman will miss the 20-over matches with a hamstring injury.
Among those joining for the last two ODIs are openers Finn Allen and Tim Seifert and pace bowler Lockie Ferguson.
The trio prioritise playing in professional T20 leagues and have not represented New Zealand in the 50-over format in the last 18 months.
Walter said the ODI series would be a chance for players to push for selection at next year's World Cup.
"We're incredibly lucky to have the depth that we do to have 21 players involved in the series," he said.
"It's also great to bring guys like Lockie, Finn, and Tim back into the one-day unit.
"For Finn and Tim in particular, we've seen what they can do in the T20 arena, and it's now a great opportunity for them to push their case in the longer format."
New Zealand ODI squad
All five games - Mitchell Santner, Michael Bracewell, Mark Chapman, Jacob Duffy, Will Young, Blair Tickner
Games 1-3 - Devon Conway, Matt Henry, Kyle Jamieson, Tom Latham, Daryl Mitchell, Glenn Phillips, Rachin Ravindra, Nathan Smith
Games 4-5 - Finn Allen, Kristian Clarke, Matt Fisher, Lockie Ferguson, Mitch Hay, Nick Kelly, Tim Seifert

item.title: Renshaw validates decade of grit with Durban ton
item.description:
Australia's Matt Renshaw celebrated his second Test century, almost a decade after his first, during the opening ICC World Test Championship tussle against South Africa.
Additionally staging a monumental 134-run ninth-wicket partnership alongside Nathan Lyon, Renshaw also pushed past his previous career best of 184 against Pakistan.
"I always wanted that second one," Renshaw told the reporters after Day 2 of the Durban Test.
"I had the monkey off the back early with that first one. I think it was like that has come in the last 10 years, all the hard work, all the failures, all the success. This was nice just for me to get."
Slotted at the No.5 position for the first time since his 2023 recall, Renshaw blunted the early threat to reach the end of Day 1 with just three boundaries from 115 balls. He notched his half-century off the second ball of Day 2, before negating the second new ball.
"I think once (I) took a few years out of the team, had an opportunity in 2023 and didn't take it, you probably think that you're never going to get this opportunity again," Renshaw added.
"So when I hit the ball, I was screaming at it, 'go, go, go'. It sort of all just hit me at once.
"You had Nathan (Lyon) at the other end, who was pretty emotional. So to see that, it was pretty special."
Renshaw's marathon knock also established a new venue record, setting the highest individual Test score in Durban by a batter coming in at No. 5 or lower, surpassing Kusal Perera’s unbeaten 153 for Sri Lanka in 2019.
While rain disrupted play for the second straight day, South Africa reached stumps on Day 2 at 27 for 1, trailing Australia by 363 runs. Josh Hazlewood made an early breakthrough by removing Ryan Rickelton for a three-ball duck, leaving Aiden Markram (15*) and David Bedingham (12*) to navigate through to the end of the day.
Series Schedule
First Test - October 9 to 13, Durban
Second Test - October 18 to 22, Gqeberha
Third Test - October 27 to 31, Cape Town

item.title: Hasan Mahmud becomes first Bangladesh pacer to record Test hat-trick
item.description:
Hasan Mahmud has become the first Bangladesh fast bowler to take a hat-trick in Test cricket, picking three wickets in three consecutive balls against Afghanistan on the third day of the one-off Test on Sunday in Abu Dhabi.
Hasan dismissed Ismat Alam, Qais Ahmad and Zia-ur-Rehman in the 83rd over at Zayed Cricket Stadium, becoming only the second Bangladesh bowler to achieve the feat in the longest format of cricket.
The 26-year-old ended a 23-year wait for Bangladesh’s second Test hat-trick, following leg-spinner Alok Kapali’s achievement against Pakistan in Peshawar in August 2003.
Kapali had taken Bangladesh’s first Test hat-trick against Pakistan in 2003, dismissing Shabbir Ahmed, Danish Kaneria and Umar Gul in consecutive deliveries.
Hasan first bowled Ismat for one with a delivery that moved back into the batter and passed beneath his bat. He then induced an outside edge from Qais, who was caught by wicketkeeper Litton Das diving to his right.
Zia was trapped lbw on the next ball. The on-field umpire initially rejected the appeal, but Bangladesh reviewed the decision, and ball-tracking confirmed the delivery would have hit the stumps.
The hat-trick left Afghanistan struggling at 220 for eight in 82.5 overs, trailing Bangladesh’s first-innings total of 346 by 126 runs.
Rahmat Shah was holding Afghanistan’s innings together with 86, but Hasan’s burst dealt a major blow to their hopes of closing the gap.
Hasan had taken four wickets for 39 runs in 17.5 overs, while fellow fast bowler Ebadot Hossain claimed three for 52 as Bangladesh tightened their grip on the match.

item.title: Bangladesh's untapped asset: The talent of retired military personnel
item.description:
Every year, trained and disciplined officers leave the armed forces of Bangladesh, typically in their late 40s or early 50s, with a decade or more of working life ahead.
They are not retirees in the ordinary sense. They are mid-career leaders starting over.
Having worked in people management across the services, government, and the private sector, I see this as one of our labour market’s overlooked inefficiencies.
On one side, Bangladesh corporate society regularly struggles to find disciplined, crisis-tested operational leaders.
On the other, a pipeline of exactly that talent exits the military every year and a meaningful share of it fails to land well in the private sector, not for lack of ability, but for lack of translation.
Why the transition stalls
The most common failure point isn't skill, it's translation. A resume built around unit designations, rank, and military-specific achievements communicates almost nothing to a civilian hiring manager.
The second most common failure point is authority: In a command structure, a decision is executed once made. In a corporate structure, the same decision is a starting point for discussion and officers who treat that discussion as insubordination rather than normal process tend to struggle in their first six months, regardless of how capable they are.
The third is pay. Many corporate leaders hesitate to hire ex-officers, fearing salary demands that do not fit their pay scales.
Some officers do arrive with expectations shaped by rank rather than by the market value of the role. Employers then pass over capable candidates and candidates conclude that the corporate sector does not value them.
A fourth , quieter factor is timing. Officers who begin preparing or updating their resume, researching target industries, or rebuilding a professional network only after their final parade almost always find the process longer and harder than those who start a year or more in advance.
What the country is missing
There's a cost on both sides. Employers who reject ex-military candidates as "too rigid" for corporate culture are often missing genuinely strong operational and crisis-management talent, simply because the candidate hasn't yet learned to present it in commercial language.
On the other hand, officers who assume their military record will speak for itself are leaving real value on the table.
Where better pay, connectivity, and corporate skill-development opportunities do not materialize, many turn to construction, tender, and supply businesses, or settle abroad.
These are legitimate choices, but when made for lack of alternatives, they are a loss to a country that spent decades training these leaders.
What would help
Closing this gap doesn't require lowering any bar. It requires three things happening earlier than they currently do:
Services headquarters can hire corporate trainers, HR practitioners, and consultants to run sessions on CV translation, interviews, corporate culture, networking, and realistic salary expectations.
What determines for a successful second career is whether it's paired with humility about a genuinely different working culture and a willingness to relearn how influence and communication work outside a chain of command.
For Bangladesh's corporate sector, HR functions, and training bodies, there's a clear opportunity here: Structured transition support -- even something as simple as mentorship pairing with serving corporate professionals could turn a currently inconsistent outcome into a reliable pipeline of strong operational leadership.
There are fair objections; public placements must not disadvantage other qualified civilian candidates.
A voluntary national register of retired personnel willing to be recalled or re-employed in emergencies such as disasters, national emergency, public health crises, general election etc should be introduced for the future. None of the discipline, crisis competence, or leadership built over a military career disappears at retirement.
The talent is already there. What's missing, in most cases, is the bridge.
Nesar Ahmed Julius is a former Navy Commander and Senior HR Consultant at a Dhaka-based HR and workplace management consultancy firm.

item.title: Cheap eats, dear lives
item.description:
According to a global study published by Visual Capitalist using data from Numbeo, Bangladesh officially boasts the cheapest dining-out costs on the planet.
At an average of $1.63 (around Tk195 to Tk200) per meal, eating out here costs less than anywhere else in the world, undercutting neighbouring South Asian peers and standing in stark contrast to Switzerland, where a simple meal will set you back upwards of $31.
On paper, this sounds like an absolute victory for Bangladeshi food lovers. We are, after all, a nation whose social life revolves entirely around food.
Whether celebrating a job promotion, catching up with old friends, or simply trying to survive a long workday, our answer is almost always to find a table and order something delicious.
Yet, anyone who actually lives here, earns in Taka, and navigates local markets knows that the $1.63 figure tells only a fraction of the story.
In reality, dining out in Bangladesh is no longer a cheap luxury -- it comes at a steep price.
The cost is paid twice: First, through the unrelenting squeeze of domestic inflation on household wallets, and second, through a systematic compromise on food safety that imperils our long-term health.
The economy of the Tk200 meal
To understand why "cheap" is a relative term, one must look at the macro picture through a micro lens -- specifically, the average Bangladeshi wallet.
An international dataset calculating prices in US Dollars fails to account for real purchasing power, local earnings, and the relentless rise in the domestic cost of living.
Over the past few years, essential commodity prices in Bangladesh have surged. Basic food ingredients -- edible oil, onions, spices, poultry, and rice -- have seen price hikes that stretch household budgets to their absolute limit.
For low- and middle-income earners, whose real wages have not kept pace with soaring inflation, even a seemingly modest meal out is a major decision.
When a single plate of rice, dal, and fish at a basic roadside hotel climbs from Tk120 to over Tk200, it represents a substantial slice of a worker's daily wage.
What looks like a negligible $1.63 to a global index is, in local terms, a growing financial burden.
For lower-income families, eating out was once an affordable respite; today, it is an increasingly stressful expense.
For the middle class, frequenting casual diners, trendy cafes, or neighbourhood joints now requires conscious budgeting.
The margin for discretionary spending has shrunk, making the claim that "Bangladesh is the cheapest place to eat out" feel less like a badge of honour and more like an ironic punchline.
Culinary bliss in a toxic matrix
If the financial side of the equation strains the wallet, the hygiene side strikes directly at the body.
The second -- and far more dangerous -- cost of dining out in Bangladesh is paid in health hazards, short-term gastrointestinal distress, and long-term medical bills.
Consider our beloved street food culture. Nothing beats the immediate sensory bliss of a plate of crisp fuchka drowning in tangy, spiced tamarind water, or a bowl of piping hot, savoury chotpoti laced with green chilies and boiled eggs.
On a chilly evening, a rich bowl of slow-cooked haleem , topped with fried onions and ginger juliennes , feels like pure comfort.
Yet, behind that intoxicating flavor profile lies a chaotic and completely unregulated production chain.
The sour water used in fuchka is often mixed using unboiled, untreated tap water.
The oil used to fry the fuchka shells or roadside snacks is frequently black, burnt, and reused dozens of times over, turning every bite into a cocktail of trans fats and toxic chemical compounds.
The raw herbs and spices sit uncovered on dusty street corners, gathering exhaust fumes and bacteria throughout the day.
It is culinary bliss, no doubt -- but it is unadulterated bliss that hampers the human body in both the short and long terms.
A single evening of street food indulgence can trigger acute gastroenteritis, food poisoning, or severe acidity before sunrise.
Over months and years, regular exposure to adulterated dyes, toxic industrial oils, and heavy metal contaminants sets the stage for chronic kidney complications, liver toxicity, and cardiovascular disease.
The cost-cutting trap
It is easy to point fingers at street vendors, but mid-range casual restaurants, cafes, and upscale fine-dining establishments are far from innocent.
Driven by rising raw material prices, high commercial rents, and squeezing profit margins, many sit-down establishments routinely resort to reckless cost-cutting measures.
Instead of absorbing high ingredient costs or raising prices transparently, kitchens often quietly downgrade their standards.
Refrigerators are overstocked or turned off off-hours to save electricity, leading to subtle food spoilage.
Meat and poultry stored well past their shelf life are heavily marinated in aggressive spices to mask sourness.
Cooking oils are recycled until they turn into sludge. "Fresh" salads are washed in municipal water straight from the tap, and kitchen staff rarely operate with basic sanitary protocols like gloves or hairnets.
The result? The elegant ambiance and air-conditioned comfort of a modern cafe offer no immunity against foodborne illness.
Diners pay premium prices only to contract food poisoning, typhoid, or gastric distress -- proving that whether you eat standing next to a rickshaw stand or sitting on a plush velvet sofa, the underlying health hazards remain remarkably similar.
Every now and then, mobile courts and food safety authorities launch high-profile anti-adulteration drives.
They fine popular eateries, slap warnings on shops, and broadcast raid videos to the public. But these drives function merely as temporary performance art.
Fining a restaurant Tk50,000 today does not fix the broken supply chain tomorrow.
Without continuous, systematic enforcement, institutional oversight, and strict cold-chain regulations, restaurants simply treat occasional fines as an operational tax and revert right back to unsafe practices.
Reality check
It is time to look past international rankings and face reality.
A meal in Bangladesh might rank as the cheapest on a global chart, but when factored against local income, food price inflation, and the inevitable medical bills that follow poor hygiene, eating out is no bargain.
Finding cheap food loses all its charm when the money saved on dinner is spent on antibiotics, saline drips, and doctor consultations.
Ultimately, saving a few bucks while eating out means absolute nonsense if you don't survive the meal to live and tell the lesson.
Until systemic reforms bring clean ingredients, fair pricing, and uncompromised food safety to our tables, every meal out in Bangladesh remains a high-stakes gamble -- one where our money, our stomachs, and our lives are all on the line.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Trump’s trade wars sting US manufacturers ahead of midterms
item.description:
For Doug Rende, who runs an aluminum product manufacturer in the US state of Ohio, President Donald Trump’s tariffs have meant millions of dollars more in annual costs -- and recently, the Iran war has made shipments even more expensive.
Rende is chief executive at Shapes Unlimited, one of many American producers smarting from Trump’s economic policies as midterm elections approach.
“Frustrating would be one word,” Rende told AFP.
“And I think that we’re sensing a lack of trust in not only the administration but the governmental process, the role of Congress to rein in executive power,” he added.
Since returning to the presidency in January 2025, Trump has wielded executive authority to slap tariffs on various products and countries.
Besides aluminum, the duties hit steel and autos too, while US trading partners face additional tariffs that vary by country.
Even as some American manufacturers have benefited as their foreign competitors encounter higher barriers, others struggle with ballooning costs and persistent uncertainty.
Trump’s spiraling trade fight with Canada and war with Iran have only deepened worries.
Grievances over Trump’s trade policies are among fault lines that Democrats hope will work in their favor as they push to flip control of the Senate and House of Representatives in November’s vote.
Rende’s company in North Jackson, Ohio, makes and distributes aluminum building products used in fixtures like fences.
Trump’s tariffs on aluminum have steadily climbed, from 10% during his first presidency to 25 percent and then 50 percent last year, and Rende has felt the impact.
“This year alone, it’s upwards of $4.5 million to $5 million in additional costs,” Rende said.
“There’s only so much that the end consumer is willing to eat,” he added. “So, we absorb a healthy portion.”
These added costs include steeper transportation fees, as fuel prices surged with the US-Israel war on Iran. Surcharges are “upwards of $6,500 per container” of goods from suppliers, Rende said.
As a result, he has paused recruitment for new jobs while investing in more robotic assembly.
Sam Miller, another Ohio manufacturer who makes kitchen and bathroom products, has been hit on both fronts in Trump’s trade wars, paying tariffs on imported materials from Asia while finding it harder to expand into Canada because of trade tensions.
“It’s been difficult for businesses to manage,” Miller told AFP from his factory floor in Warren as a machine hummed nearby, cutting countertop material. ”I do think that there will be a shift away from Republican views.”
Although Miller received refunds after the Supreme Court struck down many of Trump’s duties, the US leader has since reinstated many of them.
Deteriorating US-Canada ties add to his challenges, with Washington and Ottawa slapping tariffs on each other’s products after trade negotiations collapsed in August.
“We’re selling into Canada and it is particularly straining on both us and our customers,” Miller said.
He originally planned on opening a distribution facility in Canada this year, but progress has slowed.
Guy Coviello, president of the Youngstown Warren Regional Chamber, told AFP he is monitoring tariffs, the Iran war and immigration very closely.
These are a “mixed bag” for firms but negative overall, said Coviello, whose business group has some 3,000 members.
Some firms have lost customers or had to downsize, he said.
Canada is also Ohio’s biggest export market, with a third of Ohio’s exports going to the country.
“Where it gets even more complicated is that there are some goods that go back and forth across the border multiple times,” he said.
The Iran war adds to stresses, raising freight costs and hitting aluminum supplies due to drone attacks in the Middle East.
With a lack of new US aluminum smelters, Coviello said: “We are all for tariffs for critical items such as defense and medical industry.”
But he added: “We have to be careful when you’re talking about products that are not crucial and are not available in the US.”

item.title: ‘Going bankrupt’: Iran shopkeepers struggle as war dims demand
item.description:
At a Tehran bazaar where fragrant herbs and spices whet the appetite, shopkeeper Nasir says locals once bought his nuts by the kilo but soaring prices caused by the US-Iran war have eaten into sales, leaving businesses fighting for survival.
The marketplace in the Iranian capital’s north would usually be abuzz with customers, but shops now sit mostly empty with only small numbers of people walking its old narrow paths, a jarring shift for the sellers shouting to promote their goods.
“There used to be customers who bought two to five kilograms. Now, they’re down to buying one kilogram or half a kilogram,” said the 61-year-old.
“Prices are truly high. We all know it, and it would be a lie to say otherwise.”
Nasir called on authorities to stabilise the currency so businesses could plan ahead.
“We’re left in limbo, everyone is,” said the fruit and nut seller.
“They need to stabilise the dollar exchange rate.”
Iran’s economy has been battered by years of sanctions, but the conflict that began in February with US-Israeli attacks and an American blockade of the country’s ports has put extra strain on daily life.
Rising inflation, nearly 90% year-on-year in September according to official figures, and erratic currency exchange fluctuations have driven up the cost of everyday items. Food prices have more than doubled since last year.
At the bazaar, a historic covered market in Tehran’s Tajrish square, locals surrounded by Iranian flags and Persian signage try to escape the economic gloom, scanning sweets, jewellery, traditional garments and cuts of meat before their weekend begins.
In an alley, a street artist plays a guitar while another drums his hands on a box to draw tips from passersby.
But across the commercial district, many struggles to see a future for their businesses.
“It is a desperate, last-ditch struggle. Manufacturers are going bankrupt, laying off staff and closing shops, and the impact inevitably reaches us,” said Ali Nowruzi, 36, who runs a sportswear shop in the bazaar.
The businessman now orders only a few items for display on his shop’s shelves to stop them from looking bare like his warehouse, which he says lies empty due to lack of demand.
“We have absolutely no plan for the future. When people don’t come to buy... it effectively spells bankruptcy for the business,” he said, citing rising rent and utility bills.
“We just need some stability.”
Many shoppers, whose purchasing power has weakened since the outbreak of war, are seen leaving the bazaar without buying anything.
Azadeh, a 45-year-old woman currently out of work, says she just goes there to “watch the shops”.
Mounting pressure over the war saw Iran’s GDP contract 10.1% year-on-year between late March and late June, according to official figures.
The rial traded at around 2.7 million to the dollar on the unofficial market in the past week, compared with about 1.7 million before the war.
The minimum monthly wage that stood at around $120 a year ago has fallen to $65.
The country’s economy minister has rejected predictions of an imminent economic collapse, accusing Iran’s foes of trying to fuel public anxiety and drive up exchange rates.
Azadeh offers a price comparison of a kitchen cloth bought several months ago for 22 cents. She says that item now costs $1.10, five times more.
“It shows that prices haven’t just gone up -- they’ve truly skyrocketed,” she said.
She has stopped buying some fruits and says she can no longer afford holidays.
“We aren’t meant to just exist, we’re meant to actually live, right?” she asked.
Car mechanic Mojtaba Rezaei says his customers have “dropped to a tenth of what it was” because “goods now cost two or three times as much”.
“I actually feel embarrassed telling prices to customers. People just come in, ask the price, and leave,” the 57-year-old told AFP at the bazaar.
“So many things -- buying clothes, going out for leisure, dining at restaurants -- have all been cut out of our lives.”

item.title: Sri Lanka invites Bangladesh’s Moshiur Rahman Shanto to SL Mice Expo 2026
item.description:
Bangladeshi author, radio jockey and media personality joins international media representatives from 27 countries at Sri Lanka’s major business tourism event Sri Lanka Mice 2026.
Bangladeshi author, radio jockey and media personality Moshiur Rahman Shanto participated in SL Mice Expo 2026 in Sri Lanka following an invitation from the Sri Lanka Convention Bureau, representing Bangladesh at an international gathering of media professionals and industry stakeholders.
Held on October 5-9, the event brought together international media representatives and professionals from the meetings, incentives, conferences and exhibitions (Mice) industry.
With participants from 27 countries, the expo provided a platform for international networking, destination promotion and discussions on the future of business tourism.
For Shanto, the invitation represented an opportunity to strengthen professional connections beyond Bangladesh and engage with international media professionals in a setting where tourism, communication and cross-cultural collaboration intersect.
As a writer, broadcaster and storyteller, Shanto has built his career around connecting with audiences through conversations and human-interest narratives.
His participation at SL Mice Expo 2026 reflects his continued interest in taking Bangladeshi stories to international platforms while exploring opportunities to bring global perspectives to audiences at home.
From radio broadcasting to international media
Shanto began his writing journey in 2010, developing an interest in storytelling that eventually expanded into broadcasting, journalism and digital media.
Over the years, he has worked across several platforms, building a professional identity that combines literary expression with audience engagement.
His broadcasting career includes work with ETV News and prominent Bangladeshi radio stations, including ABC Radio 89.2 FM, Dhaka FM 90.4 and Radio Dhoni 91.2 FM.
Through programs such as Dhoka, Be Positive and Police Diaries, he explored different styles of radio presentation, from engaging conversations to narrative-driven programming.
Radio has remained an important part of his professional identity. For Shanto, the medium offers more than entertainment; it provides an opportunity to understand people, communicate ideas and bring personal experiences to a wider audience.
His work as an author complements that approach. Through books and other storytelling projects, he has continued to explore human experiences, personal struggles and the journeys that shape people's lives.
His English-language books, Highway and No Finish Line, represent an extension of his interest in reaching readers beyond the Bengali-speaking audience.
The publications also align with his broader ambition to build connections with international readers and storytellers.
A platform for global connections
SL Mice Expo 2026 offered Shanto an opportunity to interact with professionals from different countries and backgrounds.
Bringing together international media representatives and business tourism stakeholders, the event created a setting for exchanging ideas, developing professional relationships and exploring potential collaborations.
The Mice sector plays an important role in international tourism by attracting business travellers, conference delegates, exhibition participants and corporate groups.
Beyond its economic contribution, the industry can also facilitate cultural exchange and create opportunities for countries to strengthen their international visibility.
For media professionals, events of this nature offer access to stories that extend beyond traditional tourism coverage.
They provide opportunities to explore how destinations develop their identities, attract international visitors and build relationships with global markets.
Shanto's participation placed him among the international media representatives attending the Sri Lankan event.
It also offered an opportunity to develop contacts that could potentially support future interviews, media productions and cross-border storytelling initiatives.
His interest in international media engagement is closely connected to his ambition to interview people from different professional and cultural backgrounds.
Through English-language conversations and biography-focused storytelling, he aims to document the experiences of individuals whose work and achievements offer lessons for wider audiences.
Taking Bangladeshi stories beyond borders
In an increasingly connected media landscape, the boundaries between local and international storytelling continue to evolve.
Digital platforms, international events and cross-border partnerships have created new opportunities for writers and broadcasters to reach audiences outside their home countries.
Shanto's participation in SL Mice Expo 2026 reflects this changing landscape.
Rather than limiting his work to a single medium, he has pursued opportunities across radio, literature, journalism and digital storytelling.
His professional interests also include developing international conversations through media initiatives such as Legacy Makers, a platform focused on documenting the life journeys of successful individuals.
The concept reflects his belief that personal stories can connect people across nationalities, professions and cultures.
For Bangladesh, greater participation in international media networks can create opportunities to share the country's stories, introduce its creative professionals to overseas audiences and encourage collaboration with international partners.
Shanto's presence at the Sri Lankan expo formed part of this broader effort to expand his professional network and explore new opportunities for international engagement.
Looking towards a wider stage
The invitation to SL Mice Expo 2026 marks another international engagement in Shanto's professional journey.
His work across broadcasting, literature and storytelling provides a foundation for exploring new forms of media collaboration and reaching audiences through multiple platforms.
As he continues to develop his international profile, his ambitions extend beyond participating in global events.
He aims to build meaningful professional relationships, conduct conversations with influential voices from different countries and create stories that resonate with audiences across borders.
For a media personality whose career began with writing and developed through radio and journalism, international engagement represents an opportunity to connect those experiences with a wider world.
At SL Mice Expo 2026, Shanto joined media representatives from 27 countries in an environment focused on international collaboration and business tourism.
His participation highlights the opportunities available to Bangladeshi media professionals seeking to expand their reach, exchange perspectives and contribute to a more connected global storytelling community.

item.title: Gadget & Gear officially launches iPhone 18 series in Bangladesh
item.description:
Gadget & Gear, Bangladesh's only Apple Mono Store Partner and Apple Authorized Reseller, has officially launched the iPhone 18 Series in Bangladesh.
The launch event, held on Sunday October 11, marks the arrival of Apple's most advanced iPhone lineup in the country, available through Gadget & Gear stores and online.
Setting this launch apart from a standard product release, Gadget & Gear is offering complimentary Shield+ protection with eligible iPhone 18 Series purchases.
Shield+ provides a one-year extended warranty on top of Apple's standard coverage, bringing total warranty protection to two years.
It also covers up to one front-screen replacement and up to one back-glass replacement during the coverage period.
For customers Shield+ means greater peace of mind, knowing that their device is protected against some of the most common accidental damage and costly ownership concerns.
To mark the occasion, Gadget & Gear is offering a range of attractive launch benefits.
Buyers can avail up to Tk20,000 cashback on EMI, 0% EMI for up to 24 months, and a trade-up bonus of up to Tk10,000.
As an exclusive launch gift, qualifying customers will receive either AirPods Pro 3 or AirPods 5, subject to stock availability.
Additional complimentary gifts include an Apple official case, a 20W Apple adapter, and a Spigen screen protector.
All offers, eligibility criteria, and combinations are subject to applicable terms and conditions.
The launch event was attended by officials of Gadget & Gear; Rakin Absar, content creator, and Sadia Ayman, actress.
Commenting on the launch, Tasrif Khaled, head of marketing of Gadget & Gear, said: "At Gadget & Gear, we have always believed that buying a premium device should come with a premium ownership experience. With the iPhone 18 Series launch, we are proud to introduce Shield+ as a complimentary benefit for our customers, offering extended warranty coverage, screen protection, and back-glass replacement in one comprehensive package. This is our commitment to ensuring that every customer who walks out of a Gadget & Gear store does so with complete confidence in their purchase."
The iPhone 18 Series is now available at all Gadget & Gear stores across Dhaka, Chittagong, Sylhet, Narayanganj and through the Gadget & Gear online platform.
